description:
We’re a pair of aerospace engineers with strong astrodynamics skills and Python experience. We’re passionate about lunar and space exploration. We’re looking for someone who can help us design an intuitive UI/UX, someone with xp using API's that help us connect the ephemeris and terrain data, and maybe a physicist to help us with the Moon-Earth-Sun calcs.

If you're up for it, send us an email.
summary:
ILARGI (meaning “Moon” in Basque) is an interactive app designed to be a useful tool for both the engineering and educational worlds, the two most important pillars for the present and future of space exploration. Our idea is to merge both worlds in the same space: ILARGI.

The science branch of our app does not aim to substitute the more advanced tools that mission planners have and use daily. Instead, it is a quick support tool that allows easy visualization and comparison of different landing sites (L/S), providing accurate data on, among other things, their sunlight and communication windows. Although it is not meant as a substitute, that does not mean its simulations are inexact: as a team, we believe there is no room for compromising precision, so we use ephemeris and LOLA data to simulate the conditions of each L/S on the Moon as faithfully as possible.

The educational branch, on the other hand, has been given the same amount of thought as the science branch, if not more. It aims to be a great tool for cultivating the curiosity of future generations, so we made it interactive and engaging for them. Teachers around the world can use it as a classroom complement and parents can use it at home too. It is easy to use and can spark a newfound hobby in a future astrophysicist or be the starting point for a future astronaut. Additionally, as a hook, we have included a minigame that can serve as a simple introduction to the Moon and the space physics world.
details:
0. Source Code

If wanted you can explore the complete code made for the project in our GitHub repository: https://github.com/ChristianGonper/ilargi

1. What does it do?

We will divide this explanation into two sections: the Mission Analysis (M/A) and the educational.

The M/A does the following. The user faces three options: load a preexisting landing site (L/S) from NASA’s previous missions, load a previous search or make a new search. For this last one the user is asked to enter the following: position of the L/S in spherical coordinates (lat, lon, z), where z is the height from the spherical lunar surface; the beginning and end dates (duration) and the time-step for the ephemeris calculations.

With that information the Sun’s and Earth’s trajectories are simulated and different parameters of interest are obtained: the different windows of sunlight and Earth visibility; the percentage of time in which there is combined visibility of the Sun and the Earth; the duration of the different nights, highlighting the longest one; the eclipses that occur, with their timestamps, including the percentage of Sun covered; the incidence angle of the Sun (important for the Solar Arrays power budget) and lastly, the percentage of lunar resources that can be found in a 150x150 km area around the L/S.

Additionally, the user can toggle on/off the lunar resources zones present on the Moon such as: Water Equivalent Hydrogen (WEH), Aluminum (Al), Calcium (Ca), Iron(II) oxide (FeO) and Thorium (Th).

The educational section has simplified functionalities. It focuses on the different L/S on the Moon’s surface. It’s intended to be used as a support tool in a classroom but also has interesting functionalities to explore on their own. The information shown is reduced and the two main simulations are one of the illumination of the Moon so that they can visualize Moon phases and another one of the Moon’s orbit around the Earth and the Sun.

There’s also a toggle on/off section so they can learn about the presence of water on the Moon.

Kids can also explore a “Did you know...?” section with Ilargi, our mascot, who tells them interesting facts about the Moon. In addition to that we have included information about landers (based on the IM-1 Odysseus) for older children who want to expand their knowledge.

Finally, we’ve included a minigame where they can select one of the L/S and land on the surface. After a successful landing, interesting information about the L/S appears.

2. How does it work?

The physics backbone of ILARGI works as follows, in a simplified way. We use ephemeris data from SPICE to calculate the precise trajectories followed by the Earth and the Sun as viewed from the L/S on the Moon's surface during a defined time period. From an East-North-Up (ENU) reference system situated on the L/S, we implement a terrain mask made from the LOLA sensor data so that we can calculate the precise moments of the earthsets and sunsets, also with the positions in the sky of both the Earth and the Sun we can find when the Earth passes in front of the Sun.

This same engine is used by both the M/A and the educational section, so the simulations that children explore are based on the same ephemeris and LOLA data used for the mission analysis.

3. What benefits does it have?

As mentioned before, our program aims to be a support web app, something mission planners can turn to in order to quickly visualize key aspects of their future mission. It is meant to be used to confirm the suitability of the selected L/S area or to rapidly compare two or more proposed L/S and their most important characteristics.

Our other core goal is to ignite the flame of interest in children so that they can learn in an interactive manner. We imagine the following situation: a teacher wants to explain the Moon, but many of the apps available on the internet are either too hard for their students to understand or too easy. ILARGI is built to cover a wider age group, with different information for younger children in primary school as well as for older students in high school.

4. What is the intend impact of the project?

As we said in the summary, we intend to be a tool helpful in Mission Analysis first. With the information, mission planners can discard unsuitable sites early and focus their detailed analysis on the most promising ones, saving time and resources in the first stages of a mission. Having sunlight, communication windows, eclipses and nearby resources in one place makes it easier to understand the conditions of a landing site at a glance, without having to configure complex tools for every question, and to justify why one site is a better choice than another.

This also lowers the barrier for early-stage L/S studies, and makes the information easier to share inside a team, including people who may not be specialists in orbital mechanics. In the long run, we hope ILARGI becomes a habitual first step before the more detailed tools are used.

Our second goal is to have an impact on the people who will plan those missions in the future. Many of them will have their first contact with the Moon through a classroom, and we want that contact to be interactive and memorable. By learning about the Moon phases, the presence of water or how a lander touches down, children can discover that the same ideas that drive a real mission are within their reach.

Having both worlds in the same app lets the interest of one feed the other.

5. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

The easiest way to explain the tools behind ILARGI is to follow the path of the data, from the Moon to the user’s screen.

Everything starts in the scientific engine, written in Python (3.13). To know where the Sun, the Earth and the Moon are, we use SpiceyPy, the Python wrapper of NASA’s NAIF SPICE, which gives us high-precision ephemeris, light corrections and lunar reference frames. To know how the terrain blocks the view from an L/S, we read the LOLA elevation models with Rasterio and project them with PyProj. NumPy then traces the horizon over the lunar curvature and calculates the visible or eclipsed fraction of the Sun and Earth discs, while Pandas manages the time series and the geochemistry datasets. Matplotlib, together with SciPy, is used to export static images of the lunar terrain.

Those results reach the browser through a REST API built with FastAPI and served with Uvicorn, with Pydantic checking every request so that the scientific data stays consistent.

On the client side, the application is written in TypeScript, with React for the interface and HTML5 and CSS3 for the structure and custom design of the M/A panel, the educational environment and the minigame. Three.js (WebGL) renders the lunar globe in 3D with real relief, solar and Earth illumination, orbits and spacecraft models. Plotly.js draws the interactive scientific charts, such as the elevation over time, horizon profiles and sky trajectories, and the native Canvas 2D API runs the real-time physics of the minigame’s descent and landing. Lucide React provides the icons and Vite compiles and packages the frontend.

Behind this path there are also the tools we used to build and check it. Git and GitHub were used for version control, uv for the Python packages and npm (Node.js) for the web ones. Automated tests with pytest and tsx check the code, while Ruff and Prettier keep it formatted, running automatically with pre-commit before each commit. The final results were validated against the JPL Horizons API, as explained in the validation section. During the development we also used Super Intelligence (SI) tools, which are explained in their own section.

The visual side of the project was also made by the team: our mascot Ilargi was created from a photo of the Moon taken by one of our team members and edited in Canva, and the project video was edited with iMovie and DaVinci Resolve.

The datasets we used are listed in the data section of our submission.

6. How did we use Super Intelligence (SI)?

Throughout the whole development of ILARGI we used Super Intelligence (SI) tools, mainly as agents that helped us write the code. The models of the Gemini, GPT and Grok suites worked inside T3 Code, an agentic development environment (ADE), while Cursor was used as the code editor so that we could visualize the changes they made. To speed up the work, we used different Git worktrees, so that several agents could work in parallel, each one on its own pull request.

To make sure the work was reliable, we applied a peer review method: the work of each agent was reviewed by two other models, which also controlled the browser to check the final result directly on the app. Apart from writing the code, the agents also downloaded the data from the original sources, always keeping track of where the information came from, so that every dataset in ILARGI can be traced back to its origin.

Additionally, we used Claude for information searching, and Hex, a local speech-to-text tool by Anomaly, so that we could talk to the SI instead of having to type everything.

Although the code was written with the help of SI agents, every decision in the project was made by our team. We told the agents what to implement and in which order, reviewed that the physics they added was correct, and decided the path the project had to follow at every step. The UI design was reviewed until it looked as we had imagined it, and the minigame idea, including how it should behave, was defined by us. In short, all the decisions that were not internal code were made by the team.

7. How did we validate our results?

As we said in the summary, as a team we believe there is no room for compromising precision, so we wanted to make sure that the results given by ILARGI are reliable. To do so, we compared our ephemeris calculations with JPL Horizons, NASA’s online ephemeris service, which is widely used as a reference in the space community.

We asked Horizons for the positions of the Sun and the Earth as seen from three points on the lunar surface: one on the equator, one at mid-latitude and one near the pole. Then we compared them with the ones obtained by ILARGI. To make the comparison fair, both were configured in the same way: a spherical Moon with a radius of 1,737.4 km, the same light-time and aberration corrections and no atmosphere.

The results show differences of only 2.45 to 2.47 m in the position of the Earth, which is about 384,000 km away, and of 9.26 to 9.35 m in the position of the Sun, which is about 150 million km away. Regarding their position in the sky, the differences in azimuth and elevation are within 0.00122 arcseconds, while the Sun’s disc measures about 1,900 arcseconds as seen from the Moon. In other words, the error is less than a millionth of the size of the Sun in the sky of the L/S. These cases are included in our automated tests, so they can be run again after every change in the code.

It is important to note that Horizons uses the DE441 ephemeris while ILARGI uses DE440s, both from the same family of models. This means the comparison confirms that our implementation of SPICE is correct, rather than being an independent measurement of the real positions.

8. What would we improve with more time?

This section will be divided in three and it’s intended to show ideas and improvements to the M/A tool, the Educational tool and the Game we had no time to implement.

Regarding the M/A tool. The first improvement we could not add was using the location of the 3 DSN stations for calculating the comms windows of the L/S as well as indicating which and when each of the 3 stations is at the moment watching the site.
Additionally, we believe one crucial thing we failed to implement is an alternative L/S generator. One of the main ideas we thought was really interesting to add was a way to help in the search for alternatives when the original mission had been delayed. In a X km radius we would calculate, in the new date range, similar or better alternatives to the original L/S. This would be made with a weighted function; this could be a basic one made by the program, based on general characteristics or give an option to the user for implementing its own function. With that data, the program would search for L/S in the area and give them a punctuation 1 to 10.

Regarding the Educational tool, we would like to enhance the initial overview of the global lunar map by displaying the names of major craters. 

Secondly, we plan to expand ILARGI’s contextual tips by integrating a 'Learn More' button. While the initial pop-up offers a concise, accessible info, clicking this button will unlock deeper scientific context. This progressive approach keeps the interface clean for beginners while rewarding curious users with technical depth. 

At last, we intend to incorporate data of upcoming lunar missions—such as NASA’s Artemis program, VIPER, and commercial CLPS landers. By clicking on any targeted landing site on the map, users will access a mission profile detailing the responsible space agency, projected timeline, onboard instrumentation, and the specific scientific experiments or ISRU technologies to be tested on the surface. Also, in the game section we would add these new landing possibilities and give the pertinent context.

Lastly, regarding the minigame the idea was to continue the story with the landing and using a base construction to introduce the different lunar resources present with the addition of a new radioactive element: Hamburgurium. The win state would be being able to craft in the end a Burger.
